sections.skill: Explain what banks and credit unions do with deposits and loans

questions.prompt: Maya deposits $500 of her summer earnings at a bank. What does the bank usually do with much of the money while it sits in her account?

choices.text: Lends part of it to other customers, such as car buyers or businesses
Keeps her exact bills in a locked box with her name on it
Sends it to the government until she withdraws it
Invests all of it in the stock market on Maya's behalf, and she keeps any gains

questions.correct_answer: Lends part of it to other customers, such as car buyers or businesses
questions.intro: A bank is a business that accepts deposits (money people put in accounts) and makes loans (money it lends and expects to be paid back with interest). Banks keep only part of their deposits as cash and lend much of the rest. The interest borrowers pay helps the bank pay its costs, earn a profit, and pay interest to savers.
questions.feedback: Banks pool deposits and lend much of the money to borrowers. Maya can still withdraw her $500; the bank keeps enough cash and reserves on hand to meet withdrawals.

misconceptions.B: Thinks a bank stores each customer's own cash separately
misconceptions.C: Confuses a bank deposit with a tax payment
misconceptions.D: Confuses a bank deposit with an investment account

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes a credit union?

choices.text: A not-for-profit financial cooperative owned by its members
A government office that issues credit cards
A company that only sells stocks and bonds
A bank owned by outside investors who buy its stock and are not its customers

questions.correct_answer: A not-for-profit financial cooperative owned by its members
questions.intro: A credit union offers many of the same services as a bank: checking and savings accounts, debit cards, and loans. The difference is ownership. A credit union is a not-for-profit cooperative owned by its members, who are its account holders. To join, you must meet its membership rules, such as living in an area, working for an employer, or belonging to a group.
questions.feedback: Credit unions are member-owned, not-for-profit cooperatives. Profits are returned to members through lower fees, lower loan rates, or higher savings rates.
questions.topic: Banks, credit unions, and what they do

misconceptions.B: Thinks "credit" in the name means the government provides credit
misconceptions.C: Confuses a credit union with a brokerage firm
misconceptions.D: Describes a stock-owned bank, not a credit union

questions.prompt: Jordan wants to join Riverside Teachers Credit Union, but Jordan is not a teacher and has no family member who works in a school. What is the most likely obstacle?

choices.text: Credit unions do not offer checking accounts
Jordan must buy stock in the credit union on a stock exchange
Credit unions only accept customers who already have a credit card
Jordan may not meet the credit union's membership rules

questions.correct_answer: Jordan may not meet the credit union's membership rules
questions.intro: Every credit union has a "field of membership": the group of people it is allowed to serve. It might be employees of certain companies, people who live or work in a county, or members of an organization. Family members of current members can often join too. Some credit unions let almost anyone join by first joining a partner organization.
questions.feedback: A credit union can serve only people within its field of membership. Jordan should check its eligibility rules or look for a credit union whose field includes Jordan.

misconceptions.C: Thinks a credit card is required to open an account

questions.prompt: A city has a large national bank, a local community bank, a credit union, and an online-only bank. Which feature is TRUE of all four kinds of institutions?

choices.text: They can offer federally insured deposit accounts
They are all owned by the customers who keep accounts there
They all have branches where you can deposit cash in person
They all guarantee a profit on money you invest with them

questions.correct_answer: They can offer federally insured deposit accounts
questions.intro: Banks come in different types. National and regional banks are large and have many branches. Community banks are smaller and local. Online banks have no branches; customers use an app, a website, ATMs, and mobile deposit. Deposits at federally insured banks are protected by the FDIC, and deposits at federally insured credit unions by the NCUA, up to legal limits.
questions.feedback: Federally insured banks (FDIC) and credit unions (NCUA) can all offer insured deposit accounts. Ownership, branches, and fees differ from one institution to another.

misconceptions.B: Credit union ownership applied to every institution
misconceptions.D: Confuses insured deposits with guaranteed investment returns

questions.prompt: Priya keeps $1,200 in cash in a shoebox. Which risk would a federally insured bank account reduce?

choices.text: The money buying less in the future because prices rise
Having to pay sales tax when she spends the money
Spending the money on things she does not need
Losing the money to a fire or theft at home

questions.correct_answer: Losing the money to a fire or theft at home
questions.feedback: Insured deposits are protected from loss at home and from bank failure up to legal limits. An account does not stop prices from rising and does not decide how she spends.

questions.prompt: Aiden puts $40 into his savings account. What is this called?

choices.text: A withdrawal
A loan
A fee
A deposit

questions.intro: A deposit is money you put into an account. A withdrawal is money you take out. A loan is money a lender gives you that you must pay back, usually with interest.
questions.feedback: Putting money into an account is a deposit. Taking money out is a withdrawal.

questions.feedback: Taking your own money out of your account is a withdrawal; you do not owe it back.

questions.prompt: Which choice describes interest from a SAVER'S point of view?

choices.text: Money you pay the bank each month to keep your savings account open
The amount you first deposited
A tax on savings accounts
Money the bank pays you for keeping your money in an account

questions.correct_answer: Money the bank pays you for keeping your money in an account
questions.intro: Interest works in two directions. A borrower pays interest to a lender for using the lender's money. A saver earns interest from a bank, because the bank uses the saver's deposits to make loans.
questions.feedback: Savers earn interest; borrowers pay interest. The first amount deposited is the principal.

questions.prompt: Why can a bank afford to pay interest to savers?

choices.text: It charges borrowers a higher interest rate than it pays savers

It charges savers a fee equal to the interest
It prints new money to pay interest

questions.correct_answer: It charges borrowers a higher interest rate than it pays savers
questions.feedback: A bank earns more interest from loans than it pays on deposits. The difference helps cover costs and profit.

sections.skill: Online banks, apps, and partner banks

questions.prompt: A payment app advertises "bank-level" accounts. Its fine print says, "We are a financial technology company, not a bank. Banking services are provided by Harbor Bank, Member FDIC." What does this mean?

choices.text: The app company is itself an FDIC-insured bank, so it is fully protected
No money in the app can ever be insured
Harbor Bank guarantees the app company's profits
Harbor Bank holds the deposits; the app company itself is not a bank

questions.correct_answer: Harbor Bank holds the deposits; the app company itself is not a bank
questions.intro: Many apps that hold money are not banks. They are financial technology ("fintech") companies that partner with a bank. Money may be FDIC insured only if it is actually deposited at the partner bank in the customer's name and the records are kept properly. If the fintech company itself fails, getting access to money can take time.
questions.feedback: The fine print says the deposits are at Harbor Bank. FDIC insurance protects against Harbor Bank failing, not against the app company failing.
questions.topic: Banks, credit unions, and what they do

misconceptions.A: Takes the advertising at face value
misconceptions.B: Ignores insurance through a partner bank
misconceptions.C: Misreads what a partner bank does

questions.prompt: Which question is MOST useful to ask before keeping a large balance in a payment app?

choices.text: Is my balance held at an FDIC-insured bank in my name?
How many millions of people already use and trust the app?
Does the app have a nice design?
Can I send money to friends instantly?

questions.correct_answer: Is my balance held at an FDIC-insured bank in my name?
questions.intro: Deposit insurance covers money in deposit accounts at insured banks. A balance kept in a payment app may not be a bank deposit at all, depending on how the app holds it. The app's terms explain where the money is held.
questions.feedback: Whether the balance is a deposit at an insured bank, in your name, decides whether deposit insurance can apply.

questions.prompt: An online bank pays 4.0% on savings and charges no monthly fee, but it has no branches. A local bank pays 0.5% and has a branch near Ana's job. Ana is paid in cash tips each night. Which drawback of the online bank matters MOST for Ana?

choices.text: The online bank's savings rate is too high
Online banks are not allowed to give customers debit cards
Online banks are never insured
Depositing cash may be difficult without a branch

questions.correct_answer: Depositing cash may be difficult without a branch
questions.intro: Online banks often pay higher savings rates and charge fewer fees because they have no branches to run. The trade-off is access: depositing cash can be hard or impossible, and help is by phone or chat. The best choice depends on how you use your money.
questions.feedback: Ana deposits cash every night, so a way to deposit cash matters more to her than a higher rate. She might use both kinds of bank.
questions.topic: Banks, credit unions, and what they do

misconceptions.A: Thinks a higher savings rate is a drawback
misconceptions.B: Assumes online banks lack debit cards
misconceptions.C: Assumes no online bank is insured

questions.prompt: Two banks are similar except: Bank A charges a $12 monthly fee unless the balance stays above $1,500; Bank B charges no monthly fee. Kai usually keeps about $400 in checking. How much more would Bank A cost Kai per year?
questions.intro: Fees add up. A monthly fee costs 12 times that amount in a year. Many banks waive a monthly fee if you meet a condition, such as a minimum balance or a direct deposit. If you will not meet the condition, plan to pay the fee.
questions.feedback: Kai's $400 balance is below $1,500, so the fee applies every month: $12 × 12 = $144.

The color of the debit card

questions.feedback: Frequent ATM users can pay fees each time they use an out-of-network ATM, so fee-free ATM access is the key comparison.
